Pongo Poetry Project’s mission is to engage youth in writing poetry to inspire healing and growth. For over 20 years, Pongo has mentored poetry with youth at the Clark Children & Family Justice Center (CCFJC), King County’s juvenile detention facility.

Many CCFJC residents are youth of color who have endured traumatic experiences in the form of abuse, neglect, and exposure to violence. These incidents have been caused and exacerbated by community disinvestment, systemic racism, and other forms of institutional oppression. In collaboration with CCFJC staff, Pongo poetry writing offers CCFJC youth a vehicle for self-discovery and creative expression that inspires recovery and healing.

Through this special monthly column in partnership with the South Seattle Emerald, Pongo invites readers to bear witness to the pain, resilience, and creative capacity of youth whose voices and perspectives are too often relegated to the periphery. To learn more about Pongo’s work of inspiring healing and relief among youth coping with mental and emotional turmoil, register for its upcoming event, What Words Can Hold, on Oct. 8 .

articles.author: Dave Schilling
paras: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull

Are you currently at an airport? Strapped to a hospital bed, with various tubes protruding from your body? Maybe you’re on a treadmill or visiting an elder care facility? Chained to a radiator in the basement from the Saw movies?

If you said yes to any of these questions, you might be watching cable news while reading this column. The 52nd season of Saturday Night Live opens inside the New York City mayor’s office. Mayor Zohran Mamdani (Ramy Youssef, reprising the role from last season) gets a surprise visit from Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson). The president, who “for some reason that no one can figure out” loves Mamdani , has braved the big El Niño storm to visit his “day one”.

Trump unloads about his busy week – banning members of the press from the White House pool, delivering apocalyptic threats to Iran at the UN, consulting with AI leaders including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg (“It made me think, wow, RFK Jr’s probably right about those vaccines, I mean, the ‘tizz in that room …”) – before being interrupted by his assistant Natalie Harp (Ashley Padilla). Acting like “the girl from Obsession, but blond”, the dangerously jealous Harp threatens Mamdani. Trump eventually convinces the mayor to let him stay and hang out in New York in exchange for $20bn for a housing project in Queens.

articles.title: ‘I turbocharged my career then pressed eject’: why couples are getting divorced later

“We don’t know anyone whose marriage hit the skids after just a few years,” Celia said, reflecting on her divorce. “Everyone seemed to cling on to their relationships for as long as they possibly could.”

The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “ System Error : Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.

When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”

articles.title: Live show: Amazon, Meta and the fight over the future of AI; Plus, is Seattle still the place to build?
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: This week: Amazon is blocking Meta’s new Muse AI assistant from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent doesn’t identify itself and violates the site’s conditions of use. We explain why the standoff is an early sign of a much bigger fight over whether AI agents can use websites and apps on people’s behalf, and why Amazon has so much riding on the answer.
For the definitive word on the issue, we ask Muse what it has to say for itself, and get an impressively sophisticated and evenhanded response.
We recorded this week’s show live at Daniel’s Broiler in downtown Seattle, in front of a room of startup founders and CEOs, at a dinner hosted and sponsored by Northern Trust .

Mike Fridgen , a longtime Seattle entrepreneur and Madrona venture partner now working on a stealth startup, joins us to talk about whether Seattle is still a good place to build a company. The conversation covers the region’s talent, its history and the debate over taxes including Seattle’s JumpStart payroll tax, which Mayor Katie Wilson’s new budget holds flat.

Then we take questions from the room. Ridge AI CEO Ellie Fields asks how business leaders can engage productively in building the region, Latch CEO Stefan Kalb asks why Seattle has less venture capital than the Bay Area and ACME Brains founder Mary Jesse asks how to get past polarization.
We close with a satellite-themed GeekWire Trivia Challenge and an unexpected announcement from Starfish Space co-founder Austin Link .
With GeekWire co-founders John Cook and Todd Bishop. Music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell.

articles.title: 'Keep Pierce Moving' Campaign Touts Major Bus Service Expansion Plan
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: South Sound transit advocates and elected officials came together Thursday night in Tacoma to officially kick off the campaign for a ballot measure that could transform bus service across Pierce County. The "Keep Pierce Moving" campaign is making the case to voters for Pierce Transit's Proposition 1, which would enable the biggest expansion of local bus service that agency has seen in decades.

With the 0.3% increase to Pierce Transit's sales tax rates that voters will be asked to approve on November 3, in return they'll see a bus system that is able to grow by 49% compared to current service levels . Bus routes to every corner of the Pierce Transit service area will get more frequent, with many routes running hours later into the evening than they currently do.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
The measure would also fund four new routes, including the return of fixed-route transit service to Northeast Tacoma for the first time since 2024.

By the time the service adjustments are fully implemented, no Pierce Transit bus routes would operate less frequently than every 30 minutes, leaving the era of the hourly bus in the dust. The result would be a quantum leap for many Tacoma neighborhoods and cities like Lakewood, Fife, and Puyallup.

"People want transit that is reliable, that is connected, and that gets them where they need to go in dignity and convenience," Laura Svancarek, executive director of Tacoma on the Go, told Thursday's overflow crowd at the Tacoma's Berliner Beerhall. "Transit brings us together."
While Pierce County has trailed its neighbors in transit funding and service levels, the need is no less acute.

"More so here in Pierce County compared to other counties, we know that we have a lot of folks that truly rely on transit service to be able to live their life and do the things that they want and need to do," Svancarek said. "Transit brings communities together. Great transit connects people to opportunities, resources, and their lives, and that's why we are so excited about this package from Pierce Transit."

While members of the campaign are very optimistic, Pierce County's track record on transit ballot measures is going to cause a lot of nail-biting on election night. In 2011, voters rejected this very same 0.03% sales tax increase by more than 10 points, a decision that led to a catastrophic 35% service cut. Pierce Transit leaders ultimately decided to advance a significant reduction in Pierce Transit's overall service area, with DuPont, Sumner, and Bonney Lake fully dropped.

After going from a peak of 600,000 annual service hours in 2008 down to just 350,000 hours per year after those cuts took effect, Pierce Transit went to the ballot a second time in 2012 in the hopes of being able to restore some service. Voters once again said no – but that time by a painfully close 704 votes out of more than 200,000 ballots cast.

"I argue this one's much better," Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello said Thursday, comparing Prop 1 to the 2012 measure. "This one's much more inclusive. This one's much more clear. I think this one's more compelling. But that one was good too. Don't get me wrong."

Mello had a front row seat to that 2012 campaign as a member of the Tacoma City Council, and put the expansion of transit service front-and-center during his campaign to lead Washington's second most populous county.
Mello also pointed out that when the 2012 measure fell short by 704 votes, more than 15,000 voters simply did not vote yes or no.

"If we get the amount of people who don't make it all the way down to the end of the ballot, who actually know what's in it for them, we really believe we win. We really believe that we win. The case is clear. We're super clear and transparent to voters about what we buy," Mello said. "We all know that transportation access is the limiting factor to folks having access to opportunity. We have an incredibly compelling and fair case. We just have to get the voters to get there."

Pierce Transit's ballot measure comes on the heels of a successful campaign to expand transit in Spokane, with voters signing onto a 0.2% sales tax increase by a three-point margin. That victory came in the face of a significant opposition campaign, largely funded by local developer Larry Stone, that spent more than twice what the Yes for Buses campaign did.

In Seattle, voters are being asked to renew the Seattle Transit Measure, bumping an existing 0.15% sales tax up to 0.3% to fund an additional 100,000 bus trips annually – with a focus on nights and weekends.

Meanwhile in Everett, local officials will be asked to sign off on the full consolidation of the city-run Everett Transit system into the larger Community Transit network, a move that is expected to bump up transit service in Everett by 50%.

Having come so close in 2012, Pierce County's transit advocates are confident that this will be the year that they can overcome history and get voters on their side. If they don't, Pierce Transit will likely ultimately be facing service cuts in the years ahead, as expenses continue to outpace revenue coming in.

"This is an amazing package," Tacoma Councilmember Kristina Walker said Thursday. "We're gonna get out to every corner of the county to make sure everyone knows how great this package is and that they need to vote."

articles.title: Pinehurst: A Light Rail Station Built by Community
articles.author: Renee Staton
paras: This Wednesday, September 30th, North Seattle communities will celebrate as Pinehurst Station opens to riders. The station, located between Northgate Station and Shoreline South/148th Station at NE 130th Street, and 5th Avenue NE is the first Sound Transit infill station (a new station on an existing line) to open. It is also a game changer in terms of light rail access for the Bitter Lake, Haller Lake, Pinehurst, Olympic Hills, Lake City and Cedar Park communities.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
The festivities for the station are especially meaningful given that the station wasn’t supposed to happen. And, if it did happen, it wasn’t supposed to open for many more years.

Sound Transit studied including the Pinehurst Station (previously called NE 130th Street Station) as part of the Northgate to Lynnwood Link Extension, and the idea was strongly supported by Seattle City Council and transit advocates . NE 130th Street/NE 125th Street arterial provides an opportunity for an easy and fast bus connection between the station and the dense and affordable communities of Lake City and Bitter Lake. The arterial also offers a less congested and much safer, more complete pedestrian experience than other east-west arterials such as NE 145th Street or Northgate Way.

In the 2013 politics of selecting stations for the initial Northgate to Lynnwood extension, NE 130th did not make the final cut. Beyond the Lynnwood terminus station, the agency selected stations at NE 145th (now 148th) and NE 185th in Shoreline and at the Mountlake Terrace Transit Center. However, Seattle leaders saw the value of a NE 130th Street station and wanted to keep the possibility alive. Then Seattle City Council President and Sound Transit Board Member, Richard Conlin, sponsored City of Seattle Resolution 31486 specifically asking Sound Transit to do a full environmental impact study of 130th Street Station to keep momentum and options for the station in the future:

Recognizing the potential for a station at NE 130th Street and holding a bit of optimism and tenacity, North Seattle community members organized to ask Sound Transit to reconsider including NE 130th Street Station in the Lynnwood Link extension.

They launched a campaign that quickly drew significant and broad support from the transit community, environmental groups, and elected officials including Seattle City Councilmember Mike O’Brien and Seattle Mayor Ed Murray . While Sound Transit did not add NE 130th to the Lynnwood Link extension, on April 23, 2015 the board approved making the Lynnwood Link “ready” for NE 130th Street Station. This meant that as the Lynnwood Link was planned and constructed, it would be done in a way that a station could still be added at NE 130th in the future.

I was the lead organizer in this effort and am still incredibly proud of what we accomplished as a community. We showed each other that through working together we can make a meaningful impact. In the process we also built stronger relationships between neighborhoods and new leaders emerged who have since led other North Seattle efforts.

As a District 5 Seattle City Council candidate in 2015, Debora Juarez saw the strong case for a NE 130th Street station and adopted the vision of completing the station as one of her three key campaign goals. Once in office, she immediately went to work.

In early 2016, Sound Transit released the proposed Sound Transit 3 (“ST3”) ballot package listing NE 130th Street Station as a “provisional” station, to be built if funding allows. This was a disappointment for Councilmember Juarez and she launched her own successful 130th effort that included an epic number of letters from the D5 community to the Sound Transit Board.

Ultimately, the Sound Transit Board included NE 130th Street Station in the ST3 ballot package without the “provisional” tag and with a target of the station opening by 2031. ST3 was passed by voters in November 2016 including broad support in North Seattle and District 5.

While excited to know the station would be built, Juarez was not satisfied that it would open years after the rest of the Lynnwood Link. In early 2020, Juarez and Seattle Mayor Jenny Durkan, who were both Sound Transit Board members at the time, convinced the full Sound Transit Board to give the green light to working on a final design for NE 130th Street Station , allocating $20 million for that work . The North Seattle community again contributed with a massive email campaign in support. With that decision, on the eve of the pandemic, the station opening timeline accelerated toward Wednesday’s opening, only two years later than the rest of Lynnwood Link.

It’s clear that rezoning for transit-oriented development will increase ridership; and, the Sound Transit Board has repeatedly noted that it expects more housing at the station given the massive investment being made.

Following the April 2015 Sound Transit Board vote, North Seattle community leaders held a well-attended meeting to launch a discussion of a rezone centered on the future station. Subsequently, the Seattle 2035 Comprehensive Plan update released in 2016 included a “Potential Village” surrounding NE 130th Street station in Growth Strategy Figure 4 in the 2016 adopted plan. And, in 2019, under Mayor Jenny Durkan, the Seattle Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) led a station area planning process for the areas surrounding the station .

Ultimately, Seattle leaders opted to attach the zoning changes to the next Comprehensive Plan update, which was technically due by the end of 2024, but delayed first by the Harrell Administration and later by legal appeals from opponents. The One Seattle Draft Plan released in 2024 proposed significant rezoning at the station, but appeals need to be resolved before the city council can adopt the plan.

I live in a single-family home in the Pinehurst Station walk zone, in an area proposed to be rezoned to LR3, and have been fully supportive of a rezone since we started the station discussion. When Cathy Moore was Councilmember for District 5, I organized a walking tour of the proposed rezone area with neighbors.

There is substantial community support for a rezone and unlike other communities in Seattle, there is no formal opposition effort to rezoning. In fact, many residents are frustrated with how long the station area planning process is taking, considering it started in 2015. Memories of the 2012 Roosevelt Station area rezone definitely give pause to Seattle political leaders looking at subsequent zoning changes.

Now that Pinehurst Station is opening and once challenges to the One Seattle Plan are resolved, I hope that we can move forward on the rezone and engage both market-rate and affordable housing providers to make room for more neighbors.

articles.title: Lily Allen Gave a Masterclass in Public Shaming at the Paramount on Thursday Night
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: It was the question echoed around the world when Lily Allen released West End Girl last fall. Madeline—introduced on the album’s fourth track “Tennis”—was immediately inducted into the harlot hall of fame, alongside Becky with the Good Hair and Jolene . West End Girl was Allen’s first album in seven years, written over a ten-day period following her split from husband, actor, and now public enemy #1, David Harbour (of Stranger Things ). While the album’s lyrics read like a diary, detailing a PUD (that’s “Poly Under Duress,” as coined by Dan Savage) relationship fraught with infidelity, the album hits on something more universal: harm caused by a passive man. “You let me think it was me in my head and nothing to do with them girls in your bed,” she coos on “Sleepwalking.” Allen highlights that being cheated on isn’t always dramatic or explosive, but often a mundane, arduous emotional path strewn with gaslighting. However, Allen gets the last word. West End Girl is a masterclass in public shaming, reminding us that it’s often the most powerful way to destroy a man who done you wrong.

We were all here for it, as a sea of polka dots, Peter Pan collars, and baby bangs filed into the Paramount Theatre last night to hear Allen unpack her revenge epic. But before we got our hearts shattered into a million pieces with West End Girl , we were warmed up by a trio of cellists, Dallas Minor, who graced the stage and provided classical renditions of Allen’s hits like “LDN,” “The Fear,” “Hard Out Here,” “Alfie,” and even “5 O’Clock,” which was famously sampled by T-Pain in 2011. The audience acted as a chorus as we sang the lyrics, projected karaoke-style on a screen above the stage. The trio closed with a joyful rendition of “Fuck You,” which the crowd chanted gleefully in a British accent.

While we waited for Allen, my sister and I sipped our Fruityloop cocktails (blood orange juice, coconut milk, vodka, and soda), which were mixed specially for the event, and, appropriately, tasted like colorful cereal and revenge. When we saw a spotted baby blue puffer jacket, as seen on the West End Girl album cover, I squealed and sneakily snapped a photo like some kind of frenzied paparazzi. One woman’s glorious Priscilla Presley-style bouffant had me scrolling for vintage-style half wigs on my phone, which, in retrospect, is the only reasonable thing to be doing while waiting for Allen to arrive.

Then, at last, the theater went dark, and Sheezus herself emerged from behind a green lamé curtain to roaring applause. She presented her incredible outfit with a twirl: a silver strapless mini dress with a giant bow on her back, just like a Christmas present, finished with chrome platform shoes. The show started just like the album, with the title track—a song about getting the lead in a play in London, but her actor husband questions the legitimacy of the offer. She gets the last laugh, as she’s now touring the world, acting out the story of his infidelity, blow-by-blow on the world’s largest stages. There were elaborate sets. There were costume changes. At times, there were actual tears falling from her eyes, forcing the audience to ask, is she acting, or is she actually getting emotional?

More highlights from the show: Allen gave the complete “Madeline” monologue in an American accent, reciting her email exchange with the now-infamous other woman. The set dressing looked eerily similar to her and Harbour’s also-infamous Brooklyn townhouse, as shown on Architectural Digest’s Open Door . At one point, a bubblegum pink vintage-style refrigerator was wheeled out on the stage; it contained a glass of water and her vape— likely matcha-flavored —which she hit on two separate occasions. During “Relapse,” Allen dumped the contents of her Birkin bag onto the stage to reveal a pill bottle, a little plastic jar of Extra peppermint gum, and a bottle of Valentino Donna Born In Roma perfume (finally, my esoteric knowledge of perfume bottles came in handy). During “Dallas Major,” a giant three-tiered cake rose beneath her until she was poised on top, a lone bride figurine. As she sang the opening lines to“Nonmonogomummy,” she tied on a pink frilly apron that read “cuck.”

By the end of the show, and thus, the album, the “apartment” had been nearly emptied. Allen stumbled aimlessly around the large, open space, singing the tracks “Beg For Me” and “Let You W/In” with an air of disillusionment and fatigue. “I will not absorb your shame / it’s you who put me through this.” The show culminated in the hopeful realization of “Fruityloop,” a dreamy song about finally freeing herself: “Wish I could fix all your shit, but all your shit’s yours to fix.” Allen sang it with a sparkle in her eye, ending with the ultimate exhale: “Finally I see / It’s not me, it’s you.”

articles.title: A rural Idaho county banned renewables. It’s having second thoughts.
articles.author: Julia Tilton, The Daily Yonder
paras: Jeff Hough did not pull any punches. What his fellow Republican county commissioners were about to do, he said to the packed courthouse, would violate America’s founding ideals. He quoted the Declaration of Independence to make his case.
The three-person commission was about to vote on an ordinance that would ban utility-scale solar and wind development in Bannock County, Idaho.
“We cannot deny the entire county the opportunity to exercise their property rights,” Hough said. “That goes against the principles this country was founded on.”
A few minutes after Hough’s emphatic speech , the ordinance passed by a 2–1 vote. Hough was the lone dissenter.

Since that consequential vote in March 2024, Hough has become the chair of the county commission and has dedicated himself to overturning that ordinance. He will soon have a chance to make that happen. This fall, Hough and the other two commissioners are set to vote on an ordinance with new language that would allow the development of solar and wind, along with nuclear energy, in the county.
The Bannock County vote is a test case of whether — and how — a community can revisit its assumptions about the costs and benefits of clean energy and decide to welcome development it once swore off.

In 2025, nearly 1 in 4 U.S. counties had some kind of ban, moratorium, or impediment to clean energy development, up from 15 percent of counties in 2023. More than 60 percent of counties with bans are rural, according to a Daily Yonder and Canary Media analysis of data from USA Today and the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University. (The Daily Yonder defines “rural” using criteria from the U.S. Office of Management and Budget .)

Bucking this national trend and reversing the ban would put Bannock County back in play at a moment when Idaho needs all the energy it can get. Idaho Power , the state’s largest utility, expects electricity demand to grow by 1 gigawatt by 2030, a roughly 26 percent leap from current levels.

“The need to build stuff now is critical to Idaho’s economic future,” said Aaron Menenberg, the Idaho policy manager for Renewable Northwest, a nonprofit working to decarbonize the region’s grid. “We can’t afford to say no to anything.”

Bannock County, nestled in a valley a few hours north of Salt Lake City and 100 miles west of Wyoming’s Teton Range, is a prime location for new power plants. It’s home to the Populus substation, a critical juncture for getting electrons onto the grid and into Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, and the Pacific Northwest. Building new power plants near a substation is cheaper, and those savings can help bring down costs for utility customers.

But the biggest opportunity for county residents, as Hough sees it, is not utility-bill savings: It’s economic development. In recent years, Bannock County’s population has grown far more slowly than Idaho’s. The county’s rural communities, meanwhile, are watching essential services disappear, and drought worsened by climate change is making it difficult for family farms to stay afloat.

Hough believes renewables would bring money into the community. Bannock County’s neighbors offer local proof: In 2024, projects in nearby Power and Bingham counties generated $909,000 and $639,000 in tax revenue, respectively. Hough wants to send a message — to the renewables industry and others — that Bannock County is “open for business,” too.

“Rural America is in a transition state,” Hough said from his office in Pocatello, the county seat, in July. “How do we make or help rural America … transition to this new way of life, so that they can thrive and prosper?”

Not everyone shares Hough’s vision of prosperity. In south Bannock County, Hough’s campaign has met with fierce opposition. Two camps exist: On one side are residents who are willing to lease their own land to solar energy developers or stand by their neighbors’ right to do so. On the other are those who are skeptical of renewables and believe that leasing land to developers is equivalent to selling out — many of them do, however, support nuclear.

Steve Criddle, a third-generation farmer and lifelong resident of south Bannock County, voiced his support for solar in 2024 before the ban passed. He described the situation today simply: “It’s confrontational.”
Bannock County’s moratorium on solar and wind stemmed from an unlikely source: Hough himself .
It was the fall of 2023, and he had just attended a conference of the Idaho Association of Counties in Boise.

At the conference, the Lava Ridge Wind Project , a 1-GW development slated for more than 57,000 acres of federal land in southern Idaho, dominated the conversation. County leaders from around the state were concerned about clean energy developers running roughshod over their communities. (President Donald Trump’s Interior Department canceled Lava Ridge in August 2025.)

The discussion got Hough thinking. Months before the conference, he had learned that several developers, including Chicago-based Hecate Energy and Moab, Utah–based Balanced Rock Power , were approaching landowners about solar projects in Bannock County.
When Hough returned from Boise, the cautionary tale of Lava Ridge fresh in his mind, he took action.
“I realized that we didn’t have any kind of ordinance,” Hough said. “So I knew they’d come in and do whatever they wanted.”

On October 12, 2023, spearheaded by Hough, the county commissioners voted unanimously to enact a six-month moratorium on large-scale energy projects. The idea was not to ban solar and wind, but simply to give the county time to regulate the developments and ensure they balanced economic opportunity with responsible land stewardship. A public hearing on the topic was set for the following February, and the commissioners would vote on the future of the moratorium in March.
But Hough’s moratorium took on a life of its own. In the months that followed, a group of concerned residents organized to make it permanent.

Rebecca Falcon led the charge. A decades-long resident of Downey, a town in south Bannock County, Falcon had been approached by Balanced Rock in September 2023 about leasing a portion of her 80 acres for solar. Appalled, she turned the company away. But Balanced Rock’s proposed Harmon Solar Project (aka Harmon I), a 300-megawatt solar facility with a 1,200-megawatt-hour on-site battery energy storage system, included her neighbors’ land. Stopping it would take more than just Falcon saying no.

Falcon and another neighbor, Dez Hauser, who had also turned away Balanced Rock, encouraged other concerned community members to show up to the February 2024 public hearing about the future of the moratorium.

By the time the hearing rolled around, residents had sorted themselves into two groups: for solar and against it. The meeting attracted such interest that it was moved from the county courthouse to a local high school auditorium in south Bannock County. The venue was still packed.
More than two dozen speakers, nearly all of them from south Bannock County, showed up to say their piece. The vast majority testified in opposition to solar.

The commissioners convened the next month to decide what to do with the moratorium. Hough voted to repeal it. The other two commissioners voted to extend it. The commissioners framed it as an additional pause to study the potential effects of large-scale renewable energy development in the county. Yet as the controversy mounted through the spring and summer of 2024, the county declined to take further action.
The ban stayed in place. Falcon, Hauser, and the other opponents had won.

Dale Lish, a grain farmer based in Downey, was frustrated with the decision. Recently retired from a career at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Lish became familiar with solar while working on projects in Idaho and Washington through the Rural Energy for America Program. He spoke in favor of the energy source at the same hearing where Falcon and Hauser expressed their concerns.

“The approach was just no to everything, which bothered me,” Lish said of the county’s decision, in a June interview on his property. “A straight-out ban — I don’t think that’s American. I think we, as private-property owners, ought to have a chance to do what we want within reason.”
In 2023, Lish signed a one-year contract with Hecate to option about 400 acres of his land for solar development. Hecate declined to renew the contract in 2024 because of the county’s ordinance.
The company has since pulled out of the county altogether. Representatives from Hecate did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

For the two and a half years since that March vote, Hough has been beating the drum of private-property rights while also trying to educate the community on Idaho’s power needs and how they might be met in Bannock County.

While the commission won’t vote until later this fall on the new ordinance, which is still undergoing public review, at least one of Hough’s colleagues may have changed his tune. Ernie Moser, an incumbent who supported the ban in 2024, said in an interview in June that his fears about solar and wind are “not as big” as they were two years ago. Still, Moser, who’s retiring from the commission at the end of this year, stressed that he wants “to do it right” when it comes to revisiting the county’s energy policy. The other commissioner, Ken Bullock, declined to comment.

May’s primary elections offered another indication of the county’s divided views. In the Republican primary, Hough faced a challenger from south Bannock County with an anti-solar platform, and though he won his race by 14 percentage points overall, his opponent captured 70 percent of the vote in Downey. No Democrat is running in the race, so Hough won’t face competition in the November general election.
This year’s results mirror those of 2024, when former county commissioner John Crowder, who voted for the ban in March of that year, won big in Downey but lost to Ken Bullock, an ally of Hough’s.
“In south Bannock County, it’s a supermajority of residents that do not want this,” Crowder said about solar development.

Steve Criddle can trace his family’s roots in Downey back to 1876, when his ancestors first filed paperwork for water rights. His grandfather farmed grain, including wheat. Criddle’s father did the same. He’s kept the agricultural heritage alive himself, but because of a changing climate, grain farming is no longer enough to sustain him.

“We don’t get enough moisture anymore,” Criddle said. The fields where he grows crops without irrigation now hardly produce enough to make ends meet. He’s turned some of his land over to cattle grazing and has worked odd jobs over the years to hold on to the farm.

articles.title: ‘Seattle’s answer to YC Demo Day’: 25 startups pitch investors from across the country at AI House
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: AI House brought investors from as far as Boston, New York, Colorado and the Bay Area to Seattle this week for something the city’s startup scene has rarely tried: a demo day meant to help bring outside money to local founders.

Twenty-five early-stage startups pitched at the event, held Wednesday at the startup incubator and venture capital fund’s offices on Pier 70. Many of them weren’t part of AI House’s own portfolio, and that was by design, said Yifan Zhang , an AI House managing director, who came up with the idea for the event.

“We all complained about not having enough capital here, but no one was doing anything about it,” Zhang said. So AI House tapped its own connections to investors in other parts of the country, she said, and “people flew in from all over for this.”

Investors in attendance included Mike Vernal , a partner at San Francisco-based Conviction; Emily Melton , founder and managing partner of Threshold Ventures; and Rob Go , co-founder of Boston-based NextView Ventures. Many well-known Seattle-based venture capitalists also attended the event.
Zhang said she wanted the lineup to show multiple sides of Seattle: startups built around real problems and revenue, and technologists doing “crazy ambitious things.”
Theo Ellis , CEO of Seattle mortgage-tech startup Friday Harbor , called it “Seattle’s answer to YC Demo Day,” a reference to Y Combinator’s showcase in the Bay Area.

Many of the city’s startups are “not necessarily in the flashiest spaces,” he said, but they have real customers and are growing fast. For his part, Ellis said, mortgage lending technology is “not exactly nuclear-powered robots landing on Jupiter, but it’s an enormous market with a lot of businesses willing to pay for it.”
Ellis told the crowd during his pitch that Friday Harbor underwrote 0.6% of all U.S. residential mortgage applications in August, and that the company is starting to raise its Series A round.

Many of the companies that pitched have been covered by GeekWire. In addition to Friday Harbor , they included Optimly , Vantari , Jinn Labs , GateIn , Casium , Orbital Robotics , Viata , Ridge AI , Caddi , Lev , Aria (formerly Alpyne Labs) and Synthesize Bio .
Others were new to us, at least in their current incarnations:

Closing the event, Jacob Colker, AI House co-founder and managing director, made his pitch to the out-of-town investors, building on the themes in his recent GeekWire guest column and a rallying cry he delivered during Seattle Tech Week in July.

The region is full of “space, science, tech, bio, health, startup builders,” he said, with far more good ideas than local investors can fund. “The reality is there’s just not enough capital in the Pacific Northwest.” That’s where the visitors come in, he said, predicting that they’ll find “great investment opportunities and great deals.”
Seattle, Colker said, “is worth your time, your investment, your focus, your energy.”

articles.title: Tech vet takes a fresh swing at the country club with a golf and social hub in old Seattle industrial space
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Inside a sprawling former industrial building just a chip shot from the Lake Washington Ship Canal, a Seattle tech veteran and his longtime friend are building the kind of golf and social sanctuary that they feel modern Seattle is missing.

Founded by tech veteran Shankar Sundaram , a former Boeing engineer and enterprise sales leader, alongside co-founder Ryan Schaffer , a University of Washington grad who also worked at Boeing, East West Club aims to reimagine the traditional country club.

Inspired by the multi-generational Indian household Sundaram grew up in as well as the close-knit neighborhood clubs of his East Coast youth, the name East West is a nod to bridging those traditional cultural values of family, community, and hospitality with a modern Pacific Northwest lifestyle.
The ultimate goal is to create a “third place” centered around genuine, family-friendly connection rather than corporate networking or status.

“A lot of the clubs in Seattle are a little bit older and maybe just built for a different time, for a different demographic, and we’ve changed,” Sundaram told GeekWire during a tour of the space this week at 10 Dravus St. in the Queen Anne neighborhood. “We don’t have six hours to go spend at a country club. We also don’t have $100,000 to go join.”
The vision for East West Club is starting to take shape across multiple indoor and outdoor spaces in what used to be a metal fabrication studio run by the late artist David Gulassa .

Spread across nearly 8,000 square feet between two buildings, the space retains its industrial roots with exposed timber beams, rich wood accents, and high concrete walls. Heavy construction on the primary building hasn’t started yet as the team awaits final permits from the city, but once built out, the footprint will feature a “golf lab” with wide indoor simulator bays and 500 square feet of digital putting space, alongside a private 19-foot immersive simulator bay.
The broader plan includes a quiet library lounge, a pour-your-own-beer wall, a café area, and a back-alley wellness nook featuring dry saunas and red-light therapy.

Sundaram, who is married to Armoire founder and CEO Ambika Singh , wants the club to serve as a convenient, family-friendly extension of members’ homes — a place where people can drop in for an hour rather than committing an entire day.
“We want you to bring as many people as you want,” Sundaram said. “We want you to host meetings here. We want you to actually come here and do your work here.”
East West Club will also function as an events space, where members can come together for curated gatherings, tastings, music, workshops, speaker events and more.

Rather than building out a full commercial restaurant, the club plans to rely heavily on local neighborhood partnerships. Sundaram is leaning on friends for advice on the café and coffee setup and talking to neighborhood spots about possible daily fare, alongside monthly curated dinners hosted by guest chefs.

“A big part of the vision for East West is to use the club as a platform to bring together some of the best of Seattle — partnering with great local restaurants, chefs, wineries, breweries, golf and fitness professionals, and other people doing interesting things around the city,” Sundaram said. “We want the experience to constantly evolve and give members new reasons to come together.”

To fund the buildout, Sundaram and Schaffer are opting for a community-driven bootstrap model rather than taking on heavy debt or institutional equity . They are capping their initial “founder” cohort at 100 members, asking early adopters to buy in upfront .

For the first tier of 25 founding members, a $25,000 buy-in covers four years of all-inclusive family membership, along with a $450 quarterly food and beverage credit. The early bet appears to be paying off: after launching a simple waitlist on LinkedIn three months ago that drew 120 sign-ups, Sundaram invited an initial batch of 14 people to tour the unfinished space three weeks ago — and 13 of them committed on the spot.

“These early folks are taking the biggest risk,” Sundaram said . “Prepaying for something is not very common… but we’re funding this through getting 75 to 100 founders . The total club capacity is 250 people, so the idea is, if every founder goes and gets two people, that’s the club .”
Subsequent founder tiers will gradually increase in price, and once the club opens its doors — targeted for March 2027 — the model will shift to standard initiation fees and monthly dues.

Members won’t have to wait until 2027 to start gathering, either. The team plans to open a temporary “Founders Clubhouse” to early members by the end of September, kicking off a full calendar of social programming, tastings, and events throughout October — including an Oct. 11 open house — while construction proceeds on the other spaces.
If the Queen Anne location reaches its 250-member capacity, Sundaram and Schaffer already have eyes on scaling the concept, perhaps with an Eastside location.

While indoor simulator technology is a core anchor of the space, Sundaram noted that golf is not the sole prerequisite for joining. Roughly half of the initial 14 founding members who signed up do not even play golf, seeing value instead in having a neighborhood spot to host friends, throw parties, or watch sports.

For those who do want to hit the virtual links, the club plans to partner with local instructors for lessons and youth programs, but the broader design caters as much to casual socializing as it does to perfecting a swing.

When asked about competition, Sundaram points out that East West Club isn’t trying to compete with commercial entertainment chains like Five Iron Golf or high-end, pure-play golf training centers like Evergreen Golf Club.

“If you just want to go hit up a sim and go have a burger and fries, there’s lots of spaces for that,” Sundaram said. “In the city, there’s nothing that’s like this. Golf is the glue, but nobody else is really bringing in this modern aesthetic.”

articles.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft AI exec joins Niantic Spatial; Allen fund names first investment chief; Zillow AI leader heads to Stripe
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: — Niantic Spatial hired Dave Citron as chief product officer. He joined from Microsoft AI, where he was corporate vice president of product on the Superintelligence team and helped build and launch Microsoft’s first frontier foundation models.

San Francisco-based Niantic Spatial, spun out of Pokémon Go maker Niantic , builds spatial AI models and services, including a visual positioning system trained in part on images crowdsourced from Pokémon Go players. The company has an engineering team in Bellevue, Wash.

The Seattle-area executive was previously senior director of product for the Gemini app at Google DeepMind and worked on Google Meet and Google Duo. He began his career at Microsoft in 2005, helping take OneDrive from its first release to more than 200 million monthly users.
“AI is remarkably good at reading and writing, but it still doesn’t understand the physical world well enough to act in it safely,” Citron said in the announcement.

— The Fund for Science and Technology , the Seattle-based foundation responsible for giving away a large portion of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s fortune, named Jane Dietze its first chief investment officer. She starts Jan. 4, 2027, after finishing the year at Brown University, where she has held that role since 2018.

Brown says its endowment grew from $3.2 billion to $8 billion over the 10 years through fiscal 2025. Her deputy, Joshua Kennedy, will succeed her. Dietze previously held investment roles at Bowdoin College, Fortress Investment Group and Columbia Capital.

The foundation launched publicly in August 2025 with a mandate to deploy at least $500 million over four years in bioscience, the environment and AI for good. It also funds the Allen Institute and Ai2 , the Allen Institute for AI.

The fund started with a $3.1 billion endowment from Allen’s estate and is expected to oversee a large portion of the proceeds from the sale of Allen’s sports teams. Its first CEO, Lynda Stuart, stepped down in May .

— Nicholas Stevens joined payments giant Stripe as head of product for agentic commerce, working from Seattle, after a decade at Zillow . He was most recently Zillow’s vice president of product for AI and data, leading product strategy for the company’s AI products and data platform.
His LinkedIn profile notes that he drove the partnership that made Zillow one of seven global launch partners for OpenAI’s ChatGPT apps platform. He previously worked in product at Prismatic.
“I believe AI buying & selling on your behalf can be magical,” he wrote.

— Scowtt , a Kirkland, Wash.-based startup that uses AI to predict which sales prospects will become customers, named Ben Trenda chief revenue officer. Trenda is an ad tech veteran who worked at Overture/Yahoo, AOL and Rubicon Project, and co-founded iSocket. Scowtt says it is approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue.

— The American Astronomical Society named University of Washington astronomy professor Emily Levesque the next editor in chief of its journals, including The Astrophysical Journal. She takes charge in August 2027, succeeding Ethan Vishniac.

— ThriftBooks , the online used-book seller founded in Seattle in 2003, named Carla Anderson Skogland chief financial officer. She had been interim CFO since April. Anderson Skogland, who is based in the Seattle area, was previously CFO of Sono Bello. She spent 11 years at Amazon, and earlier worked at T-Mobile and for more than 15 years at Starbucks.

— Michael Mann is stepping down as executive director of Clean & Prosperous , a climate policy group that backed Washington’s Climate Commitment Act, once a successor is chosen. He took over on an interim basis from the late founder David Giuliani and led the group for five years. Mann, founder of consulting firm Cyan Strategies, previously led the City of Seattle’s Office of Sustainability and Environment.

— Lani Ramos joined Yoodli , a Seattle startup that uses AI roleplays for communications training, to build its renewals function. Ramos spent 13 years at Tableau and Salesforce, most recently as director of renewal for North America.

— Former Starbucks CFO Rachel Ruggeri joined the board of San Diego-based Jack in the Box . Ruggeri, a Seattle-area finance leader, spent more than two decades at Starbucks and was its CFO from 2021 to March 2025. She also serves on the board of Stryker.

— Victor Fetter is stepping down at the end of the year as chief technology and business systems officer at Everett, Wash.-based Fortive after nearly seven years. Rich Noonan , Fortive’s chief information security and technology operations officer, will become CIO. Fetter, who is based in Mississippi, plans to expand his board work and angel investing.

articles.title: Microsoft unveils all-in-one Copilot app, taking on Anthropic and OpenAI in new push to boost adoption
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft on Friday morning unveiled its long-promised Copilot “super app” — without officially calling it that — combining AI chat, coding and long-running agents into a unified app for business and personal use.

The new version of the Copilot app adds sections called Home, which combines chat with Microsoft’s Cowork agent ; Code, which lets people build their own apps and tools by describing them; and Autopilot, where people can set up their own always-on AI agents.
It also brings full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot, so people can create and edit documents with AI and their co-workers without switching apps.

The announcement is Microsoft’s answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, which have been combining chat, coding and agents in their own apps and selling them directly to businesses that have long been Microsoft’s core customers. Microsoft also uses models from both companies in Copilot, alongside its own.

Partners and rivals: Microsoft executives contrasted the company’s approach with OpenAI and Anthropic during an event Wednesday, according to a transcript provided by Microsoft. The pitch is aimed at corporate IT departments, which have long relied on Microsoft for security and compliance.

Jacob Andreou, the executive vice president who leads Copilot , said Microsoft knew that “unlike a lot of our competition, sending your most sensitive files down to a local machine into a VM was a complete nonstarter” — an apparent reference to Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, which runs in a virtual machine on the user’s computer.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella pitched Copilot as a hedge against relying on any one AI lab, saying companies should be able to test models against their own benchmarks and swap one out for another.

“My test of true independence going forward is for you to have a private eval that you can hill climb on and substitute a model,” he said. Translation: a “private eval” is a company’s own set of tests for AI models, and “hill climb” is a phrase in vogue in AI circles for steadily improving results against those tests.
A company that can’t do those things, he added, has effectively handed the knowledge it builds with AI “to somebody else.”

Model choice: Microsoft also emphasized the ability to switch between AI models from different companies. A menu shown during the presentation let users pick OpenAI’s GPT or Anthropic’s Opus, or an Auto mode that chooses a model for each request.
Microsoft also showed its own MAI models alongside OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI on one of Nadella’s slides, although they weren’t listed in the menu shown during the demo.

The rollout: Nadella first promised the super app at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in June, saying that “come summer” the company would bring “coding to all knowledge work within one Copilot super app.” On Microsoft’s July 29 earnings call , he told investors it would arrive “this quarter,” which ends Sept. 30.
Friday’s announcement meets that deadline with less than a week to spare, and most of the new features won’t be widely available until later.
Office inside Copilot: Copilot has long run inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint. Now the full apps also run inside Copilot. “This is not just some simplified viewer,” Andreou said.

In a demo, a Microsoft product manager had Copilot pull data into an Excel workbook, accepted her team’s tracked changes in a Word document, and then had Copilot turn both into a PowerPoint deck without leaving the app. Co-workers can edit the same files at the same time from the regular Office apps, according to Microsoft.

How it’s priced: Copilot now has two ways to pay. A per-user monthly license covers everyday uses such as chat and Copilot features in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. More intensive agent work, including Cowork, Code and Autopilot, is billed based on usage, as are the newest frontier models, OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable.

“Our view is that there are two kinds of AI at work,” said Jared Spataro, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer for AI at Work, in a recorded briefing for media. “They call for two very different ways of paying, and Copilot offers both.”
Consumer Microsoft 365 subscriptions will also add usage-based billing later this year for Cowork, Code and other new features, Spataro said.

Nadella told investors in July that Microsoft is evolving its business model “beyond per-seat to per-seat-plus-consumption.” Usage-based services are off by default, and administrators can set spending limits for an entire company, specific groups or individual users through Microsoft’s Agent 365 management tools.

From OpenClaw to Autopilot: Autopilot grew out of Microsoft’s experiments with OpenClaw, the open-source personal AI agent that went viral earlier this year. In March, Nadella described OpenClaw as a security risk akin to “a virus.”

By June, Microsoft had introduced Scout, an always-on personal agent for work that it called the first of its Autopilots. Nadella told investors in July that the agent was “powered by OpenClaw.” The new Copilot drops the Scout name, and people instead create and name their own Autopilots.
In his presentation this week, Andreou pitched Autopilot as the answer to the concerns that have kept agents like OpenClaw out of big companies.
“The hallmark of an amazing, long-running agent is autonomy and flexibility,” he said. “That is the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”
Each Autopilot runs in the cloud inside a company’s Microsoft 365 environment, with its own identity, memory and email address, and people can tag it in Teams or Outlook like a co-worker.

In a demo, a Microsoft employee playing the role of a regional manager at a retail chain gave his Autopilot, named Dot, one goal: make sure stores had inventory in time for Black Friday. It chose which Teams channels, email threads and inventory data to monitor, sent him a daily summary, and flagged a shipment problem that could affect 18 stores.

The adoption question: Microsoft reported more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats in July, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats the company reported in January.

The new Copilot comes three weeks after Microsoft reorganized its financial reporting around a similar idea, creating a segment called Agents and Infra and moving GitHub’s cloud revenue into its Microsoft 365 business.
“It’s no longer about building or selling one app or service, but about connecting the entire trajectory of a ‘job to be done,'” Nadella wrote in a note to investors about the change at the time.

Microsoft 365 cloud revenue, which covers business and consumer subscriptions including Copilot and now GitHub, reached $100.3 billion in fiscal 2026 under the new structure, up about 19%. Microsoft doesn’t disclose how much of that comes from Copilot.
“None of these things really matter unless they actually go to work inside of your companies and deliver real value,” Andreou said.
Microsoft plans to share more at its Ignite conference, Nov. 17-20 in San Francisco.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Train Day!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: 2026 has been a big year for trains in Puget Sound. In January, the Federal Way Link Extension completed its first full month of operation. Simulated service on the 2 Line began in February , providing 4 minute frequencies for the first time between Seattle and Lynnwood. In March, the Crosslake Connection finally connected the 2 Line with Seattle. Link ridership jumped 46% in April thanks to the new service across Lake Washington. In May, the Sound Transit Board confirmed funding for several ST3 Link extensions (at the cost of other extensions). In June, Sound Transit welcomed passengers aboard new Sounder trains and set multiple Link ridership records . The USA vs Belgium World Cup match in early July helped Link surpass 300,000 passengers in one day for the first time ever. Last month, transit agencies in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties restructured their bus networks to cement Link as the backbone for regional transportation in Puget Sound.
To add to the list, Sound Transit is opening a new Link station and Amtrak is rolling out next-generation trains in September.

On September 30, Amtrak Cascades will welcome the first passengers aboard new Amtrak Airo trainsets. Amtrak Airo are trains built by Siemens that will soon run on many short distance Amtrak routes across the country. The first three of eight trains for the Cascades route are in Seattle and will operate on two roundtrips daily. The remaining five trainsets will enter service as they complete testing. An additional 75 Amtrak Airo trainsets will begin serving other routes around the country next year.

While the new trains will not reduce travel times or offer more daily trips, these trains can carry more passengers (over 300 seats per train), will be more reliable, and are more comfortable than the aging rolling stock currently used on Amtrak Cascades. Passengers can expect adjustable headrests, panoramic windows, enhanced lighting, and modern interiors.
Beginning September 30, Amtrak Airo trains will be used on the following Amtrak Cascades trips.
Between Seattle and Eugene: Train 503: Seattle to Eugene at 7:10am – 1:48pm Train 508: Eugene to Seattle at 4:30pm – 10:50pm
Between Seattle and Vancouver: Train 516: Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30am – 12:30pm Train 519: Vancouver, B.C. to Seattle at 4:45pm – 9:10pm

Seattle Transit Blog will share a first look at the Amtrak Airo trains on Tuesday, including pictures and videos from a trip on the train. Until then, check out this Bluesky thread with highlights from the media tour on Saturday.

Also on September 30, Sound Transit will begin service at Pinehurst station. Pinehurst station is the agency’s first Link in-fill station and is located between Northgate and Shoreline South/148th stations. This the second piece of the ST3 measure to be completed (after Downtown Redmond Link) and will be the last Link station to open until Graham Street station in 2031. Pinehurst station is served by the new Metro Route 77 which connects the station with Bitter Lake and Lake City. 1 Line and 2 Line trains will begin stopping at Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30. The very first train to serve Pinehurst is a 2 Line train that departs Wilburton at 4:04am and arrives at Pinehurst at 5:05am.

To celebrate the new station, Sound Transit is hosting an event from 2pm-6pm on Wednesday. The event will include live music, local organizations, sponsors, food, an interactive activity with station artist Romson Bustillo, and the ST Shop merchandise booth.

articles.title: The flock thickens: Starbird Chicken is coming to Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: $5 A MONTH TO HELP KEEP CHS PAYWALL-FREE Subscribe to CHS to help hire writers and photographers to cover the neighborhood. CHS is a pay what you can community news site with no required sign-in or paywall. To stay that way, we need you. Become a subscriber to help us cover the neighborhood for $5 a month -- or choose your level of support (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The mystery of new commercial life hatching in the failed 10,000-square-foot Amazon grocery on E Pike has been revealed. The arrival of Starbird Chicken on Capitol Hill will mark new energy for a block that has been darkened for two and a half years.

It will also be an example of what happens when highly optimized, fully leveraged, and fluidly designed corporate strategies cross lines, overlap, and push all their eggs into the same basket in a neighborhood with finger lickin good demographics and spending habits.

“Starbird has built something truly special by reimagining what a chicken restaurant can be, from the bold flavors and hospitable, modern restaurant design to the overall guest experience,” Vin Mehta , the Portland-based entrepreneur and franchisee leading a 17 location expansion of the chicken chain into the Pacific Northwest, said in a company press release quoted by industry tracker FastCasual.com . “Together, we’ll combine Starbird’s innovative approach with our team’s operational experience and passion for building lasting connections.”

CHS reported this summer on signs of new life in the Pike at Belmont space in the AVA Capitol Hill mixed-use redevelopment of the neighborhood’s old Mercedes-Benz dealership where the massive Amazon Go was abruptly shuttered in 2024 as part of what would become a nationwide retreat for the global giant.

This week, Starbird’s construction team filed new paperwork with details of their plans for a new 3,000-square-foot restaurant to serve the company’s tenders, wings, and sandwiches in a major chunk of the former cashier-less, tech-powered grocery space. An ambitious $620,000 base construction budget is attached.
The expansion has already been on the burner. A West Seattle Starbird is scheduled for its ribbon cutting on Fauntleroy Way SW on Monday .

Starbird is a Northern California-born, premium fast-casual restaurant chain founded in 2016 by culinary incubator The Culinary Edge , a company that operates as a gun for hire in revamping menus and operations for large national chains while also establishing its own brands.

Starbird specializes in “fresh, scratch-made food” and “always antibiotic-free, never frozen” fried chicken including tenders, sandwiches, wings, and “house-made sauces,” positioning itself around “reinventing the fast-food experience” with “feel good crispy chicken.” With an emphasis on “tech-enabled, omnichannel dining” and virtual kitchens alongside brick-and-mortar restaurants, the brand has expanded beyond California through multi-unit franchise partnerships.
The name also has a familiar ring. Yes, it sounds like Starbucks . And, hey, we’re not sure what the folks at the 1910-era Starbird Apartments around the block on Boylston will think.
One of the most recent Starbird openings was in Colorado (Image: Starbird Chicken)

The first Starbird opened in 2016 in Sunnyvale, California, on W El Camino Real a few miles from Apple Park and a shorter drive from the LinkedIn headquarters. The Silicon Valley debut served as the pilot location for the concept, testing their app-based curbside pickup model alongside standard dine-in service. Like most big chains, in-store ordering is heavily automated via digital kiosks and integrated mobile app check-ins.

Starbird’s traditional real estate footprint favors car-oriented, suburban-style corridors over dense, pedestrian neighborhoods but there a few different formats of stores. In San Francisco, Starbird developed a commercial ghost kitchen hub in SoMa, serving the area through bike and scooter couriers and delivery apps.
Capitol Hill, circa 2026 and 2027, is up to its ears in chicken joints. And the flock is growing even with the now permanent loss of neighborhood favorite Bok a Bok .

This month, CHS reported plans from Puget Sound-based Conscious Hospitality Group for a re-start of its 11th Ave restaurant space with a new roasted chicken venture fronted by celebrity influencer chef Matt Broussard . The Seattle Times gushed over the prospects but didn’t report that the plan is a re-heat. The 11th Ave space was originally the flagship location of the company’s scuttled “1,000 location,” sustainable, and tech-optimized chicken sandwich chain concept Mt. Joy.
Starbird, meanwhile, has pushed past the 20 location mark and is on a skyward trajectory.

“From day one, we saw something special in Starbird. This innovative concept is in a league all its own,” investor Greg Dollarhyde said in an announcement five years ago as the company raised $12 million in funding. “Starbird continues to beat every expectation.”
Starbird Capitol Hill is under construction at 600 E Pike. Learn more at starbirdchicken.com .

articles.title: Here are your chances to speak up on the mayor’s proposal to overcome Seattle’s $175M deficit
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council has launched its review of Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed $9.1 billion 2027–2028 budget, scheduling multiple hearings and public comment opportunities over the next two months before adopting a final plan.

Councilmember Dan Strauss , chair of the Select Budget Committee, emphasized community participation as the council evaluates funding priorities. Residents can weigh in during six regular comment sessions and two dedicated public hearings featuring both remote and in-person testimony.

CHS reported here on the Wilson proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
The council’s announcement invites the public to review the council’s Budget Basic webpage to “learn more about how they can make their voice heard.”
